2 · Academic Case
College Support Analysis
Transparency gap — per-class National Merit Semifinalists
The school reports only rolling 15-year finalist/commended totals plus individual honorees; it does not publish a
clean per-class Semifinalist count, and a Charlotte-Christian-specific Semifinalist figure could not be verified from
public reporting. This is a reporting-format gap — the school chooses a 15-year lens rather than an annual one.
Grading and the no-rank policy, as explained to colleges
The profile states plainly that the school does not rank students. GPA is on a 4.0 scale; honors courses
receive +0.5 quality point and AP/500-level courses +1.0. All upper-school courses count toward GPA; transfer
credits are shown but excluded from the cumulative GPA. To give colleges context without a rank, the profile
publishes GPA quintiles and a full grading scale, so a reader can locate a student in the class without
head-to-head ranking. A NACAC-compliant disciplinary policy is also stated.
Transparency gap — test-optional strategy and digital portfolios
Beyond naming Scoir and the required grades 9–11 PSAT, the school does not publish a detailed written
test-optional advising strategy or a digital-portfolio (video/portfolio) program for applicants. Not published is not the
same as not practiced — it is simply not documented online.
Segment confidence: ~90%
This is the strongest-documented segment. Published AP pass rates, SAT/ACT ranges, National Merit totals, the
grading scale, and the no-rank/quintile method are all in hand. The only real gaps are the per-class Semifinalist
count and a written test-optional playbook.

4 · Application Support
College Support Analysis
SEGMENT 4 OF 7
Hands-On Support: The Application Itself
Essays, letters, review, scholarships, financial-aid navigation, and internship experience.
Essays and the Writing Center
During senior year, college counselors “walk alongside” students as they submit applications and partner with
the on-campus Writing Center — a free resource where writers in grades 6–12 can get individual guidance on
application essays through short peer-tutor sessions. A summer College Essay Bootcamp is also part of the
counseling programming.
Junior Seminar (grade 11, required, ~0.5 credit)
A required junior-year course is the backbone of application preparation. Students are taught to write college
essays, build a resume, discover potential majors based on interests and strengths, learn to budget time and
money, decide which colleges to visit or apply to, and complete a mock admission-committee activity with
college representatives.
Scholarship and merit-aid track record (well documented)
Window Scholarships / awards Note

Classes of 2023–25 (aggregate) $13,875,968 115 honor graduates; 58 athletic signings
The itemized Class-of-2025 awards span presidential and leadership scholarships across a wide range of
colleges, indicating breadth across the class rather than a few outsized awards concentrated in a handful of
students.
Internships / Winterim
Winterim (late February) is the documented vehicle for internship-style experience: the 2025 edition included
20 offerings, among them 7 vocational-shadowing experiences and 10 local educational experiences, alongside
mission/service and travel options.
Transparency gaps — application mechanics and need-based aid
Several process specifics are not published: how teacher and counselor recommendation letters are optimized,
whether every application is reviewed before submission, and an explicit Early Decision / Early Action strategy
framework. On need-based aid, the school hosts a “Paying for College Night” and a financial-aid parent series, but
does not publish a written process for FAFSA / CSS Profile completion, award-letter comparison, or appeals. These
are documentation gaps — worth asking the office about directly — not evidence the support is absent.

Essay support (Writing Center + Bootcamp + Junior Seminar) and the scholarship record are well documented. The
thinner areas are the fine mechanics of letters/review/ED strategy and the step-by-step need-based-aid navigation.

CHARLOTTE CHRISTIAN
1 · Counseling Engine
College Support Analysis
SEGMENT 1 OF 7
The Counseling Engine
People, timing, and tools — who guides the college process, when it starts, and what data families get.
Charlotte Christian runs a small but clearly structured college-counseling operation. The upper school (grades
9–12) enrolls roughly 435 students and graduated about 94 seniors in the Class of 2025. Two professionals are
dedicated to college counseling — a Director of College Counseling and an Upper School College Counselor —
supported by two school (personal/academic) counselors and an upper-school registrar who also fields
athletic-recruiting record requests. Against a senior class of about 94, that works out to a favorable effective
caseload of roughly 47 seniors per college counselor for a school of this size.
When individualized counseling begins
The college-counseling program is described by the school as an individualized process that begins in ninth
grade and continues through the end of senior year. A separate college-and-career planning brochure
notes that guidance “starts in the eighth grade” with high-school course selection. Read the ninth-grade start as
the beginning of individualized college counseling, with an earlier eighth-grade course-planning touchpoint
feeding into it.
Grade-by-grade family programming (published 2025–26 calendar)
• Grade 12 College Planning Parent Night (late August) and a Transition-to-College Senior Parent Night
(April).
• Grade 11 and Grade 10 College Planning Parent Nights, plus a Rising Grade 9 Parent Night.
• A Christian College Fair (open to the community) and a Paying-for-College Night.
• PSAT administered to grades 9–11.
• A “Countdown to College” blog, authored by the Director of College Counseling, that walks families
through each step of the process.
Data and predictive tools families access
The counseling office uses Scoir as its platform for college search, application management, transcript
sending, and college-rep visit scheduling. Scoir offers scattergrams and a “Predictive Chances” feature, but
each high school controls whether students and parents can view scattergrams and how much outcome data
populates them.
Transparency gap — predictive-data visibility settings
The school does not publish its specific Scoir scattergram / “Predictive Chances” visibility settings, nor any
admission-outcome dashboards. Families cannot confirm from public sources exactly what predictive data they will
be shown. This is a documentation gap on the school’s part, not a sign the tools are unavailable — the platform is
confirmed in use. It is a good question to ask the office directly.

CHARLOTTE CHRISTIAN
7 · Fit, Rank & the Whole Class
College Support Analysis
SEGMENT 7 OF 7
The Honest Questions: Fit, Rank & the Whole Class
Rank policy, support beyond the top of the class, and genuine fit versus default-to-prestige.
Class rank
The school does not rank students — stated in every profile edition. To let colleges gauge rigor and standing
without pitting high achievers against one another, it substitutes GPA quintiles, a published grading scale, and
honors/AP weighting.
Support for students not at the top / non-traditional paths
The office’s stated mission is explicitly inclusive of all students — whether headed to a community college,
a gap year, the military, the workforce, or a four-year college. The Class-of-2025 enrolled roster bears this
out, including a community-college enrollee, a postgraduate program, a real-estate school, and a childcare
career path alongside four-year destinations. The Class of 2026 publicly celebrated service-academy
appointments, evidencing a documented military pathway.
Genuine fit vs. default-to-prestige
The required Junior Seminar frames “finding a college that will be a good fit,” and the counseling philosophy
defines a “good college” as one that provides opportunities for spiritual growth, allows families to be good
financial stewards, and prepares students for a career and calling — an explicitly fit-and-values framing rather
than a prestige framing. The Director has publicly cautioned against a perfectionist, must-succeed-at-everything
mindset.
Transparency gap — learning-differences support through the college process
The school publishes a robust personal/social-emotional counseling program, but it does not publish a formal
learning-support / accommodations program (e.g., a named learning-resource center) or a documented process for
securing College Board / ACT testing accommodations for students with learning differences. Families whose
students need accommodations should ask the counseling office directly. Absence of published detail is not
evidence the support does not exist.
If a student changes direction
The published philosophy — counselors “walk alongside” students, support non-four-year paths, and
emphasize fit over prestige — points to flexibility, though no formal protocol for mid-process pivots is published.
Segment confidence: ~70%
The no-rank/quintile approach and the fit-over-prestige philosophy are clearly documented, as is explicit support for
varied post-graduate paths. The one clear gap is a published learning-differences/accommodations pathway through
the college process.
Governing principle across all seven segments
Unpublished is not the same as deficient. Where this dossier flags that the school “does not publish” something,
that is a transparency gap on the school’s part — a question for the counseling office — never a verdict that the
program is weak in that area. Everything reported here reflects only what the school publishes and what public
research surfaced.

CHARLOTTE CHRISTIAN
3 · Institutional Leverage
College Support Analysis
SEGMENT 3 OF 7
Institutional Leverage
How the school’s name and documentation work on a student’s behalf with college admissions readers.
The School Profile as a positioning document
The 2024–25 Academic & Student Profile (CEEB 340667) is a polished two-page document built to
contextualize each student for a college reader. It explains the no-rank policy, the weighted-GPA method, GPA
quintiles, and a full grading scale (so a college can place a student in the class without a rank); it also surfaces
the Academic Conservatory Program, a Seal of Biliteracy, AP breadth and pass rates, and the school’s
association memberships.
Those memberships — alongside regional accreditation (SACS/Cognia) and Christian-schools bodies (CESA)
— notably include the admissions-professional associations NACAC, SACAC, and NACCAP. Membership in
those bodies signals to colleges that the office operates by recognized professional standards.
On-campus college-rep visits
The counseling office schedules college-representative visits through Scoir Visits and welcomes reps from
August to November, with published directions to the office. This is a rep-visit season, not an on-campus
interview program — on-campus admissions interviews are not mentioned in the published materials.
Transparency gap — documented admissions-office relationships
No special institutional relationships, feeder pipelines, or standing arrangements with particular colleges are
published. The profile and brochure list where students have been accepted and enrolled but assert no privileged
relationships. This is appropriate and expected — such relationships are rarely published by any school — and its
absence is not a mark against the program.
Segment confidence: ~65%
The profile-as-positioning function is fully documented and the rep-visit season is confirmed. The genuinely
unknowable piece — behind-the-scenes relationships with specific admissions offices — is a category that virtually
no school publishes, so its absence here is normal rather than a red flag.

### Number of AP courses — DISCREPANCY, FLAGGED

Two school-published figures conflict and are **not reconcilable** from public text:

- The **Upper School page** states *"more than 45 Advanced Placement and honors classes are
 offered."* This is an explicitly **combined AP + honors** count.
- The **2021-22 Profile** enumerates an AP/500-level list of **~23 distinct AP courses** plus a

profile omits this list):

~23-course AP list as indicative-only.

### Exam policy

- **"Students in AP classes are required to take the AP exam."** (2021-22 Profile.) An explicit
 mandatory-exam policy — this is the strong version of the policy and is worth surfacing, as it
 means the 89% pass rate is *not* self-selected down to only confident testers.
- **Placement gate:** *"Students must meet placement criteria in order to take Honors and AP level
 courses. In general, students must earn an 'A' in the prerequisite course to move up a level."*

 four years stale; the school does list Central Piedmont Community College among acceptances and

### Post-AP course depth

- **Math — genuine post-AP:** **Calculus III** (1 credit), described as *"Multivariable functions,
 vector-valued functions in plane and space, curvature, double and triple integrals, vector
 analysis, differential equations."* Prerequisite: **93% in AP Calculus AB or completion of AP

 multivariable/vector-calculus territory.
- **Physics post-AP:** Calculus III is paired on the profile with **AP Physics C: Electricity &
 Magnetism**, alongside AP Physics C – Mechanics.
- **Computer science — THIN.** The 2021-22 Profile lists a single **AP Computer Science**. The
 current curriculum page *"does not list dedicated computer science or information technology
 courses at the upper school level"*; coding/design-lab work appears as **middle school**

 research): **NOT PUBLISHED / appears not to exist.**

 **AP Spanish Literature**, AP Latin. Honors ladders run French II/III/IV, Latin II/III/IV,

### Grade-trust mechanics

**GPA weighting and quality points** (identical language in both the 2021-22 and 2024-25 profiles —
stable policy):
> *"Grade point average (GPA) is based on a 4.0 scale, with the exception that honors courses
> receive 0.5 extra quality point and AP 500 level courses receive 1.0 extra quality point. All
> (CCS) upper school courses are included in the calculation of GPA."*

- **Transfer-grade policy:** *"If a student enters Charlotte Christian with credits from another
 high school, a transcript from the previous high school will be enclosed with the CCS
 transcript. Those grades are not included in the CCS cumulative GPA calculation."*
- **Weighting-scheme change:** *"Effective with the Class of 2019, weighted courses receive 0.5 and
 1.0 extra quality points for honors and 500 level courses respectively (vs. 1.0 and 2.0 for all
 prior graduating classes)."* — i.e. the school **halved its weighting** at the Class of 2019.
 Any pre-2019 GPA is not comparable.
- **Transcripts updated in June**, at the conclusion of each academic year; two semesters per year.

**Grading scale** (unchanged 2021-22 → 2024-25):
A+ 97–100 = 4.0 · A 93–96 = 4.0 · A− 90–92 = 3.67 · B+ 87–89 = 3.33 · B 83–86 = 3.0 ·
B− 80–82 = 2.67 · C+ 77–79 = 2.33 · C 73–76 = 2.0 · C− 70–72 = 1.67 · D+ 67–69 = 1.33 ·
D 63–66 = 1.0 · D− 60–62 = 0.67 · F 0–59 = 0.

**Class rank:** *"Charlotte Christian School does not rank its students."* — stated flatly in both
profiles. **But the school does publish a five-quintile GPA table** (see Card 5), which is the
functional substitute: colleges can locate a student's band without a rank.

**"Most rigorous" course-load norms: NOT PUBLISHED.** The profile does not state what fraction of
students take the most demanding available program, nor does it publish a counselor
rigor-rating rubric.

**Honors Graduate designation (CCS-specific):** *"Recognized for earning a cumulative GPA above a
4.0 in grades 9-12."* Class of 2025: **41 Honors Graduates** out of ~94. Three-year total
(2023–25): **115 Honor Graduates.**

**Graduation requirements — 27 total credits** (2021-22 Profile, `TO VERIFY` for currency):
4 English · 4 Mathematics · **4 Biblical Studies** · 4 Social Studies · 3 Science ·
3 World Languages (or Level III) · 1 Fine Arts · 1 Electives · **1 January Term** ·
**.5 Junior Seminar** · .5 Speech · 1 Physical Education (or two seasons on varsity/JV team).
*.25 J-Term credit per year is a graduation requirement.* The **4 credits of Biblical Studies** is
the single largest Christian-specific transcript signature — it consumes elective space that
peer schools spend elsewhere.

- **Olivia Day** — US School Counselor
- **Olivia Brilhante** — US School Counselor (listed as "Olivia McCarrick" on the 2024-25 Profile
 and as "Olivia Brilhante" on the counseling brochure and Student Counseling page — **DISCREPANCY,
 FLAGGED**; most likely the same person following a name change, but the school publishes both
 and this is not confirmed)

**Roster change over time** (evidence of turnover in the second college-counseling seat):
- **2021-22 Profile:** Jodi Foxx (Director of College Counseling), **Katrina Cassier** (College
 Counselor), **Ginny Schmidt** (US Personal & Academic Counselor), Kirsten Mayers (Registrar).
- **2024-25 Profile:** Jodi Foxx (Director), **Lauren Miller** (College Counselor), Olivia Day,
 Olivia McCarrick, Kirsten Mayers.
- **Jodi Foxx is the constant** — Director of College Counseling in both the 2021-22 and 2024-25
 profiles, i.e. **at least four years in the role** as of the current profile. Her exact start
 date / total tenure: **NOT PUBLISHED.** `TO VERIFY`.
- **Counselor tenure, prior employer, and professional background (e.g. former admissions officer)
 for any counselor: NOT PUBLISHED.** No bios are published on the college counseling page.

### Counselor:student ratio — CALCULATED, TO VERIFY

The school does **not publish a ratio**. Derived from published figures on the 2024-25 Profile:

- **435 students in grades 9-12**, **2 college counselors** → **≈218:1 across the whole upper
 school**.
- **94 students in the Class of 2025**, 2 college counselors → **≈47:1 per senior class**.

`TO VERIFY` — both are **modeled by me, not school-reported.** The 47:1 senior-class figure is the
more meaningful one for application load and is the fairer comparison against peer schools that
quote a per-class ratio; the 218:1 figure reflects that the alphabet split (K–Z / A–J) assigns
each counselor all four grades. Also note the two *personal* counselors (Day, Brilhante) are **not**
college counselors and should not be added to the denominator.

### The 9 → 12 timeline of named programming

From the **College Planning Checklist** and the counseling brochure — counseling formally
*"begins in the eighth grade"* (brochure) / *"begins in ninth grade"* (website). Minor
inconsistency, flagged.

**Grades 9–10**
- Get involved in community (church, volunteer, school activities)
- Focus on college-prep curriculum; develop study habits
- Choose electives meeting graduation requirements + exploring career interests
- **PSAT 8/9 (Grade 9)** and **PSAT/NMSQT (Grade 10)** in October
- Get to know your counselors
- **Complete career assessments with your college counselor (Grade 10)**
- Named events: **Grade 9 Parent Orientation** (Aug), **Freshman Walk** (Aug), **Freshman Seminar**
 (Aug–Sep, in **WIN Lab**), **Rising Grade 9 Parent Night** (Jan, middle school),
 **Grade 10 College Planning Parent Night** (Jan)

**Grade 11 — the structural core**
- **Junior Seminar**, a *"specially-designed class for students in grade 11"* and a **0.5-credit
 graduation requirement**. In it students are taught to: **write college essays**, **prepare
 their resume**, discover potential majors based on interests and strengths, learn budgeting
 time and money, determine which colleges to visit or apply to, and **complete a mock admission
 committee activity with college representatives.**
- **Students are required to visit two colleges in the spring semester for Junior Seminar.**
- **PSAT/NMSQT in October**
- Meet college admission officers visiting CCS in the fall
- Attend **Christian College Fair** (fall) and **NACAC National College Fair** (spring)
- Talk with counselor about the **SAT and ACT testing plan**
- **Meet with your college counselor in the spring to discuss your letter of recommendation**
- **Ask 1–2 teachers to write a letter of recommendation in the spring**
- Evaluate/deepen community involvement; seek leadership positions
- Finalize the college list, *"being sure to include every possible type of college that might be
 of interest"*
- Named events: **Grade 11 College Planning Parent Night** (Sep/Nov), **Financial Aid Information
 Night** (Oct)

**Grade 12**
- **College Application Kick-off with the college counselors in August**
- Meet visiting admission officers in the fall *"to demonstrate your interest"*
- Attend the **Christian College Fair** in the fall
- **Finalize your test-optional strategy with your college counselor**, and send scores if needed
- Complete applications with counselor help
- **Work with your college counselor and the CCS Writing Center to finalize your application essay
 and supplemental responses**
- **Use Scoir to request supporting documents be sent to your colleges**
- Complete the **Self-Reported Academic Record (SRAR)** if required
- Set up and monitor applicant portals
- Attend admitted-student events in the spring
- **Optional: parents complete the FAFSA; students complete scholarship applications**
- *"Pray as a family for discernment throughout the application process"*
- Named events: **Grade 12 College Planning Parent Night** (Aug), **Financial Aid Information
 Night** (Oct), **Transition to College Parent Night** (Apr), **Senior Walk** (Apr),
 **College T-Shirt Picture** (Apr)

**Dated instances for the 2025-26 cycle** (college counseling page): Grade 12 College Planning
Parent Night **Aug 28, 2025**; Christian College Fair **Sep 22, 2025**; Paying for College Night
**Oct 21, 2025**; **PSAT Oct 22, 2025**; Grade 11 College Planning Parent Night **Nov 13, 2025**;
Grade 10 College Planning Parent Night **Jan 12, 2026**; Rising Gr. 9 Parent Night **Jan 21, 2026**;
Transition to College Senior Parent Night **Apr 9, 2026**.

### Application mechanics owned by the office

Confirmed **owned/supported**: applications (*"complete college applications with the help of your
college counselor"*), **essays** (taught in Junior Seminar + finalized with counselor **and the
Writing Center**), **testing** (SAT/ACT plan, test-optional strategy, score sends, on-campus
**standardized testing preparation classes**), **teacher recommendations** (structured spring ask
of 1–2 teachers, plus a counselor letter discussion), **financial aid** (Financial Aid Information
Night, Paying for College Night, FAFSA, parent education series *"including topics such as
financial aid and transitioning to college"*), **scholarship search** (senior scholarship
applications; the school publishes a full named 2025 scholarship inventory), **transcripts** (via
Scoir + a dedicated transcript request form), and **SRAR**.

Also published as **services provided by the counseling office** (brochure):
- Individual meetings with **all new to upper school students**
- **Personality and interest assessments**
- **Standardized testing preparation classes**
- **On-campus visits by college admissions counselors**
- **On-campus Christian College Fair open to the community**
- Parent education series (financial aid, transitioning to college)
- Post-decision support: *"how to choose a roommate or how to navigate the first few weeks of life
 on a college campus — counseling does not end once the college decision has been made."*

### Reach and tools

- **Platform: Scoir** (`app.scoir.com`) — used for transcript requests, **Scoir Visits** for
 scheduling college rep visits, and sending supporting documents. **Not** Naviance/MaiaLearning.
- **College rep visit window:** *"The office welcomes college representatives from August through
 November."* **Number of rep visits per year: NOT PUBLISHED.** `TO VERIFY` — a four-month window
 is published but no count.
- **Number of campus visits made by staff per year: NOT PUBLISHED.**
- **Published School Profile: YES** — an annual *Academic & Student Profile*, currently the
 2024-25 edition, with CEEB 340667. This is a real institutional asset (see Card 4).
- **Writing Center:** *"a free resource on campus that provides individual guidance to students as
 they complete their application essays"* — the counseling office formally partners with it in
 senior year. Referenced on site as the **Media & Writing Center**.
- **Distinctive framing:** the brochure states counselors remind families a *"good college"* is one
 that *"provides opportunities for spiritual growth,"* *"allows families to be good stewards of
 their financial resources,"* and *"prepares students for a career and calling through their
 education."* This is an explicit, published values filter on college fit — unusual to state
 so plainly and material to how the list is built.

CHARLOTTE CHRISTIAN
5 · Standing Out
College Support Analysis
SEGMENT 5 OF 7
Standing Out: Cultivating a Distinct Hook
Support for a differentiated profile, plus athletic-recruiting and arts-portfolio process support.
This is historically the thinnest area to document across schools, and Charlotte Christian is no exception at the
“hook/spike” level — but several concrete, process-level supports are published.
Athletic recruiting (documented at the process level)
The college-counseling page provides a concrete recruiting-support mechanism: college coaches seeking
records are directed to the upper-school registrar. Signing volume is published in aggregate: 21 college
athletic signees in the Class of 2025 (18 in 2023–24; 17 in 2020–21). Class-of-2025 signings span baseball,
football, golf, lacrosse, tennis, softball, soccer, swimming, track & field, and volleyball, into programs ranging
from an Ivy League university to Power-Four and regional destinations. Individual athlete names are omitted
here; figures are reported in aggregate.
Fine-arts / artistic-portfolio development
The arts pipeline is well documented: a Center for Worship and Performing Arts anchors the program,
alongside a competition drama team, mainstage musicals, 40+ arts electives, and national arts honor-society
chapters. External recognition includes regional musical-theatre (Blumey) nominations, and recent graduates
have gone on to dedicated arts institutions. This supports portfolio-relevant experience, though it is program
strength rather than documented admissions-portfolio coaching.
“Hook / spike” development
The closest published analogues to structured “spike” development are the Junior Seminar’s major- and
interest-discovery work and the Academic Conservatory Program, which awards distinctions in
Bible/Philosophy/Religion, English, Fine Arts, Math/Science, Social Studies, and World Languages (37 such
distinctions in the Class of 2025).
Transparency gap — explicit hook coaching and portfolio/audition prep
The school does not publish an explicit, process-level program for developing a distinctive applicant “hook,” and
detailed artistic-portfolio or audition coaching for the admissions process is not documented. The building blocks
(Conservatory, seminar, strong arts and athletics) are present; the packaging of them into an admissions “spike” is
simply not described publicly.
Segment confidence: ~58%
Athletic-recruiting mechanics and the arts pipeline are concrete and published in aggregate. The
differentiation/“hook” coaching layer is the least-documented element — consistent with this segment across
schools.
